## June 23, 1956 — A Saturday

You were born on a Saturday in the American summer, and on that same day in Cairo, Gamal Abdel Nasser was formally confirmed as President of Egypt. He ran without opposition. The plebiscite was a formality for a man who had already consolidated power — but June 23, 1956 was the day the confirmation was made official, the presidency locked in. You share your birthday with the moment Nasser's Egypt became Nasser's Egypt in full.

Thirty-three days later, he nationalized the Suez Canal.

---

**You were born on the eve of one of the great geopolitical earthquakes of the twentieth century.** The Suez Canal nationalization on July 26, 1956 — a month and three days after your birth — triggered a crisis that ended with Britain and France humiliated, the United States having sided against its own allies, and the world understanding for the first time that European imperial power was genuinely finished. The British Empire did not end in 1956, but the pretension that it could still act as a world power independent of American approval effectively did. You were born on the day the man who caused that reckoning was confirmed in office, weeks before he struck.

**On your exact birthday, sixty-two years earlier, the Olympic movement was founded.** On June 23, 1894, Pierre de Coubertin convened a congress at the Sorbonne in Paris and established the International Olympic Committee. The first modern Olympic Games followed in Athens in 1896. You were born on the 62nd anniversary of that founding, and in the year of the Melbourne Olympics — the 1956 Games, held in November and December, which became famous for the bloody water polo match between Hungary and the Soviet Union, played weeks after Soviet tanks had crushed the Hungarian uprising. That match was not sport. It was war continued by other means, and the crowd at the pool knew it.

**The Hungarian Revolution came four months after your birth.** On October 23, 1956, students and workers in Budapest rose against Soviet rule. For days it seemed the uprising might succeed. Then Soviet tanks rolled back in on November 4th, and the world watched and did nothing. Two hundred thousand Hungarians fled as refugees. You were born into the year that showed what the Iron Curtain actually was — not a metaphor but a military fact, enforced by armor, and the Western alliance would not contest it.

**The sky above your childhood contained radioactive fallout.** In 1956, both the United States and the Soviet Union were conducting atmospheric nuclear tests — detonating weapons in the open air, releasing radioactive material that circled the globe in the jet stream and settled into soil, water, and food. Strontium-90 was appearing in children's teeth and bones. The anti-nuclear movement was just beginning to name what was happening. You grew up breathing and eating the residue of weapons tests. Every child born in the 1950s did. It would take the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty of 1963 — when you were seven — to move the tests underground.

**The television set had just become ordinary.** By June 1956, a majority of American homes had a television. The tipping point had passed. You were born not into the novelty of television but into its dominance — a world where the living room already organized itself around the screen. The medium that would carry Kennedy's assassination, the moon landing, Vietnam, Watergate, and everything that followed was already the furniture of daily life before you arrived.

---

**The arc of a lifetime.**

You are seventy years old in 2026. Born in the year Nasser nationalized Suez, Soviet tanks crushed Budapest, and radioactive fallout drifted unseen through the atmosphere.

You were seven when Kennedy was assassinated. Thirteen when the moon landing happened. A teenager through the entirety of Vietnam. Twenty when Saigon fell. Twenty-three when the Iranian Revolution overthrew the Shah and the world's understanding of the Middle East was rearranged. Thirty-three when the Berlin Wall fell — old enough to have grown up believing it was permanent, young enough to still build a life in what came after.

The internet arrived in your late thirties. The smartphone in your early fifties. The COVID pandemic in your sixty-third year.

The Suez Crisis that was set in motion thirty-three days after your birth is now taught as Cold War history. The Hungarian Revolution that happened four months after your birth is now a chapter in textbooks. The atmospheric nuclear tests that salted your childhood are now a regulated memory. The world that produced all of these — tense, divided, genuinely terrified of its own weapons — gave way, across the span of your life, to something different and in many ways unimaginable from the vantage of that June Saturday in 1956.

You have been present for the entire transformation.
